name: Assyrtiko

lines.s10: Assyrtiko is the white of Santorini: lemon, sea salt and wet stone, bone dry, with acidity that makes your mouth water.
lines.s20: Assyrtiko comes from the volcanic island of Santorini, where the vines are coiled into baskets on the ground to hide from the wind. The wine is bone dry and tastes of lemon, sea salt and crushed rock, with a sharp, mouthwatering finish.
lines.s45: Assyrtiko is a white grape grown on what is left of a volcano: the hot, dry Greek island of Santorini. The vines stand in ash and pumice, each coiled into a basket on the ground against the wind. The wine tastes of lemon, underripe peach and sea salt, with a stony edge. It is bone dry, and its acidity stays piercing even in that heat. Most sees only steel, and a riper, oaked style is called Nykteri. Assyrtiko is made for oysters, grilled octopus or a whole fish with lemon. The vines grow on their own roots, because the pest that ruined Europe's vineyards cannot live in the ash.
lines.sale: Assyrtiko is the nearest thing to squeezing a lemon over the plate and adding a pinch of sea salt. Have it with the Gulf oysters tonight, raw or chargrilled, and you will not reach for the lemon.

glass.lead: Lemon, underripe peach and quince over sea salt and crushed volcanic rock, bone dry, with piercing acidity on a sturdy frame.

ladder.where: Mainland Greece: Macedonia, Thrace and the high Peloponnese
Santorini, a hot, dry, windswept island of volcanic ash

glass.structure: Bone dry. Acidity high and piercing, alcohol medium plus to high, body medium and sturdy; mostly unoaked.

home.home: Santorini, a hot, dry, windswept island in the Aegean. The vines grow on their own roots in volcanic ash and pumice, woven into low baskets called kouloura against the wind. Dry Santorini is at least 85 per cent Assyrtiko, mostly made in steel; Nykteri is the riper, oaked style, and Vinsanto the sweet wine of sun dried grapes.
home.abroad: Across mainland Greece and on other islands it keeps its crispness, with more open fruit and a less dense build. Beyond Greece it is a rarity: Australia's Clare Valley has grown a little since the 2010s.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; an oaked Nykteri or an old bottle a little warmer.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a wider bowl for Nykteri or a bottle with some age.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary. A young, tight Santorini opens with a few minutes of air in the glass.
service.age: Three to eight years for dry Santorini, longer than a hot island suggests; Vinsanto far longer.

with.why: the wine's lemon and salt season the oyster
piercing acidity against char and oil

with.dish: Whole grilled sea bass or bream
with.why: it does the work of a squeezed lemon
salt meets salt, and acidity matches the tomato

labels.means: The island's protected name: a dry white of at least 85 per cent Assyrtiko, with Athiri and Aidani.
A riper dry Santorini aged at least three months in oak; the name recalls the old night pressing.
Santorini's sweet wine of sun dried grapes, at least 51 per cent Assyrtiko, cask aged and unfortified; one word.
The low basket into which each Santorini vine is woven, sheltering the grapes from wind, sand and sun.

guest.q: How can a wine from such a hot island taste so sharp?
guest.a: Assyrtiko is the rare white grape that holds its acidity in a hot, dry climate. The island adds the rest: sea wind, old vines and poor volcanic ash keep the wine taut and salty.

guest.q: I usually drink Chablis. Will I like this?
guest.a: I think so. It has the same lean, stony feel with no oak in the way, but it is saltier and sharper, with more weight behind it.

guest.q: Is Vinsanto the same as the Italian Vin Santo?
guest.a: No. Vinsanto, one word, is Santorini's sweet wine, from Assyrtiko and Aidani dried in the sun. Vin Santo, two words, is Tuscany's, from other grapes dried indoors. Santorini's is never fortified.

compare.tell: Chablis, which is Chardonnay, is softer at the edges and less salty, with green apple and chalk; Assyrtiko is sharper and sturdier, with lemon pith and sea salt.
Dry Riesling is more perfumed, with lime, jasmine and, with age, petrol on a lighter body; Assyrtiko shows stone and salt in their place, with more alcohol and weight.
Albariño is lighter and more perfumed, with white peach and apricot; Assyrtiko is firmer and more austere, with less scent and more salt.

cards.front: Assyrtiko blind: what parts it from Chablis and from dry Riesling?
cards.back: Salt and stone on a sturdier, stronger frame with piercing acidity. Chablis is softer at the edges and less salty; dry Riesling is lighter and more perfumed, with lime and jasmine and no salt.

cards.front: Name Santorini's three wines of Assyrtiko, and what sets each apart.
cards.back: Dry Santorini, at least 85 per cent Assyrtiko, mostly unoaked. Nykteri, riper, with at least three months in oak. Vinsanto, sweet, from sun dried grapes, at least 51 per cent Assyrtiko, aged two years or more in cask.

cards.front: Why do Santorini's Assyrtiko vines grow on their own roots?
cards.back: Phylloxera cannot live in the island's volcanic ash and pumice, which hold no clay, so the vines were never grafted. Many are very old.

questions.q: A blind white is pale and star bright, bone dry and unoaked: lemon pith, underripe peach, sea salt and crushed rock, with piercing acidity yet real alcohol and weight. Which grape and origin fit it?
questions.exp: Piercing acidity with salt and stone on a sturdy, fairly strong frame is Assyrtiko from Santorini. Chablis is softer at the edges and less salty, at lower alcohol.

questions.q: A guest orders a glass of Vinsanto from Santorini after dinner and asks how it becomes sweet. What do you tell her?
opts: The grapes are dried in the sun before pressing
Grape spirit is added to stop the fermentation
Noble rot shrivels the grapes on the vine
The grapes freeze on the vine and are pressed frozen
questions.exp: Vinsanto is made from late picked grapes, mostly Assyrtiko, laid in the sun for a week or two and then aged in cask. It is never fortified, so no spirit is added.

questions.q: A guest has read that Santorini's vines are woven into baskets that lie on the ground, and asks what the baskets are for. Which answer is right?
opts: To shelter the grapes from wind, sand and sun
To keep phylloxera away from the roots
To let machines pick the fruit
To hold rainwater around the trunk
questions.exp: The kouloura shelters the fruit from the meltemi wind, blown sand and sun. Phylloxera is kept away by the volcanic ash itself, which holds no clay, and not by the basket.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Santorini, with mainland Greece and the other islands as the nearer abroad and the Clare Valley the one New World planting the entry names.
The say line follows the Codex's own respelling in the Greece record, ah-SEER-tee-ko; the Court's grid holds none for this grape.

No Codex record is contradicted. The profile, the dials and the region records for Santorini and Greece supplied lemon, underripe peach, quince and pith, the salt and volcanic rock, beeswax with age, the kouloura and what it does and does not protect against, the own rooted vines in ash and pumice, the 85 and 51 per cent rules, Nykteri, Vinsanto and three to eight years of age.

The mainland's style (the same crispness with more open fruit and a less dense build) is Wines of Greece's own wording for Assyrtiko outside Santorini; the moderate rung of the ladder (lemon zest, green apple, orange blossom) follows it and published notes on wines of Macedonia, Thrace and the Peloponnese.

The Clare Valley: Wine Australia's regional guide dates the first Australian planting to 2012, and other accounts give 2010 or 2011 and a first wine between 2014 and 2016, so the entry says only since the 2010s. Small plantings in California and South Africa are reported in one source each and were left out.

Santorini as what is left of a volcano, and old vines, are common knowledge the Codex's Santorini record supports (volcanic ash and pumice, own rooted vines); the date of the eruption was left out for want of a source read here.
Honey beside beeswax in the age group is a taster's reading; the reviewed profile names beeswax alone.
Gulf oysters are the one dish from the Creole table.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after five fixes. The rules of the protected name, Nykteri, Vinsanto, the own rooted vines and the Clare Valley were confirmed; one absolute about Tuscany was false, the long line could be misheard in two places, and one tell leaned on notes the entry lists as its own.
changed: guest[2].a: Vin Santo, two words, is Tuscany's, from other grapes. Neither is fortified now reads Vin Santo, two words, is Tuscany's, from other grapes dried indoors. Santorini's is never fortified. Tuscany has a fortified Vin Santo, labelled liquoroso, so neither is fortified is false. The true difference a guest can use is the drying: in the sun on Santorini, indoors in Tuscany.
lines.s45: A guest was never told the grape is white or Greek, and It followed the vines and then Nykteri, so the ear took the wrong subject twice. 110 words.

glass.ladder, the moderate rung: lemon zest, green apple, orange blossom now reads lemon zest, green apple, white peach. The mainland wine is described as fruitier and milder, not as floral, and every tell in the entry says Assyrtiko has less scent than its neighbours.

compare, the Riesling tell: Dry Riesling shows lime, white peach and, with age, petrol on a lighter body now reads Dry Riesling is more perfumed, with lime, jasmine and, with age, petrol on a lighter body. Lime and white peach are among this entry's own notes, so they cannot part the two. The reviewed confuse line gives Riesling its flowers and lime; the tell now says so.
cards[0].back: dry Riesling is lighter, with lime and white peach and no salt now reads dry Riesling is lighter and more perfumed, with lime and jasmine and no salt. The same tell, on the card.
open: White peach beside underripe peach in the stone fruit group, and honey beside beeswax, are the author's reading.
How a mainland Assyrtiko differs is put two ways in the sources (fruitier and milder; richer and less mineral). The entry says more open fruit and a less dense build, after the Greek wine body.
Whether Nykteri carries the same 85 per cent floor as the dry wine is put both ways; the entry gives no figure for it.
No source address could be opened from this session: winesofgreece.org does not resolve from here.
